answer: activate (Operational mode) is one verb over many targets: activate swimage activates the currently installable image and implies a system restart (db-action auto|empty-db|upgrade-db|rollback, default auto; optional label; -f skips the confirmation prompt). activate database activates the currently inactive database, also implying a restart (db-instance active|manual|oneday|onehour|oneweek|rollback|temp, db-passphrase string 40..200, restart-type cold|warm default cold, sanity-check-override true|false default false). activate location-led starts an LED location or lamp test on a chassis or card (led-mode flash|solid, default flash; timeout 0..120 s, default 0 meaning no timeout; only one test at a time). activate eqpt-fw activates a firmware image on a chassis/card/tom (resource plus fw-image-name). activate krp installs a Key Replacement Package. activate otdr and activate otdr-fiber-check trigger OTDR measurements, activate loopback enables WSS loopback on an NMC, and activate activate-file activates a file. For the database case there is also a separate command: activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>], which activates an available database snapshot. Its pre-condition is that a snapshot must have been taken (see take-snapshot); db-instance defaults to temp, paraphrase is a string of length 40..200, and sanity-check-override defaults to false.

capabilities is the per-card one: show capabilities-<name>, where name is the card name (string); it retrieves the capability information of a card. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. l0-capabilities is the photonic one: show l0-capabilities takes no parameters at all and shows the capability details related to the node's Layer 0 functions. oadm-capabilities is the add/drop one: show oadm-capabilities [max-degrees] [max-adgs] reports the maximum number of degrees (uint8, value 20; 0 if not supported, and degrees are only supported on OADM node types, ILA being 0 by convention because it has exactly 2 fixed directions) and the maximum number of Add/Drop Groups (uint8, value 110; 0 if not supported, ADGs also only on OADM node types). The note in the guide is that max-degrees is the maximum working degree-number, not necessarily the supported deployment configuration. All three are show-only and run in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode.

show controller-card-<name> displays just the controller card, with redundancy-status (active, standby, not-in-service; default not-in-service), redundancy-standby-status (ready-synchronized, not-ready-synchronizing, not-ready-synchronize-fail, lock-out, card-not-present; default not-ready-synchronizing), number-of-switchover-events (uint32) and time-of-last-switchover (both only visible on the active controller), and additional-details (string 0..128). card is the generic card-base object with attributes common to every card type: add/set/show/delete card-<name>, with required-type, required-subtype, card-mode, chassis-name, slot-name, subslot-name (settable only at creation), power-profile, category, admin-state (lock/maintenance/unlock, default unlock), oper-state, avail-state, alarm-report-control (default inhibited), alias-name, label, parent-card, subcard-list, last-reboot-reason and last-reboot-time. For what a model of card supports, use show supported-card-<card-type>, which reports node-type-compatibility (all/ILA/OADM), supported-subtype, default-card-mode and supported-card-mode, card-width, card-height, is-field-replaceable, category, grid-mode-support, max-power-draw, leds, location-led-support, console-port-support, support-serdes-config, supported-bands and supported-features. All three are available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

macsec-entity is the Ethernet MACsec object: add/set/show/delete macsec-entity-<name> with supporting-facility (an ethernet facility), enabled (true/false, default true), link-security-control (must-secure or should-secure, default must-secure), replay-protection (enable/disable), replay-protection-window (0..4294967295, default 0), alarm-report-control (default inhibited) and label. Its cipher term is read-only: negotiated-cipher-suite on show; the configurable cipher choice lives in mka-policy (macsec-cipher-suite, plus key-server-priority, confidentiality-offset and sak-rekey-interval). secure-entity is the optical-line/L1 encryption object: add/set/show/delete secure-entity-<name> with supporting-facility and remote-secure-entity (the remote optical carrier on 1830 GX G40, the remote ODU on G30, or the remote OTUFlex for CHM7/CHM7x L1 service encryption), enabled (default false), re-key-frequency (3600..86400 seconds, default 28800), re-key-fail-policy (kill-traffic or continue-traffic, default continue-traffic) and traffic-kill-offset (0..86400 s, default 0, used only when the policy is kill-traffic). Its cipher terms are read via show secure-entity-sa-proposal-<name>/<number>: encryption-algorithm aes-gcm-16, encryption-key-length key-length-256, integrity-algorithm none, dh-group ecp-521.

ase-idler-service is the ASE idler filling function on a card: add/delete/set/show ase-idler-service-<name>, with ase-idler-enable (enabled/disabled, default disabled) to switch ASE idler filling of the unused and nmc-failed portions of the band spectrum, and the read-only ase-idler-state (ase-enabled, ase-partially-enabled, ase-faulted, ase-disabled; default ase-disabled) reporting whether filling is complete, incomplete or faulted. Its function is idler, and in SLTE that means the ASE idler functionality handled at the RD WSS even though the signal comes from elsewhere. ase-idler-source is the pump that produces the signal: set/show only, with pump-enable (enabled/disabled, default disabled), the read-only pump-state, target-output-power (-3.00..20.50 dBm, default 13), admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), and supporting-input-port and supporting-output-port. Its function value is ase-idler-source. sw-service does not belong with them: it is a software command, show sw-service-<sv-name> / show sw-services, listing OS services and containers with equipment, location, state (off/ok/fail), state-details, cpu-usage, memory-usage, uptime, last-start-time and reboot-count.

No, they are not harmless. change-ztp-mode [-f] [ztp-mode=]<enabled|disabled> toggles Zero Touch Provisioning: change-ztp-mode enabled starts ZTP, reverts the database to the factory default and triggers a system reboot. change-ztp-mode disabled disables ZTP and stops it if it is already running; the command can be run while ZTP is in progress, interrupting it. Use -f to skip the confirmation, and show ztp to read the current mode. clear [-f] recover-mode clears the recover-mode flag, which confirms the current configuration as is, re-enables communication with the line cards and potentially reconfigures the traffic settings, so the guide states it may be traffic impacting. It takes no parameters. By contrast the carrier-mode commands are read-only: show golden-carrier-mode-<card-type>/<carrier-mode> and show supported-carrier-mode-<name>/<carrier-mode> only display carrier-mode information (capacity, client-mode ethernet or ethernet-otn, baud-rate, application, compatibility-id, status, supported-subtypes). Both change-ztp-mode and clear recover-mode are Operational mode only.

third-party-app shows and sets the application itself: set/show third-party-app-<app-name> with version, vendor, product, label, state (running, stopped, failed; default stopped), information (string 0..1024) and enable (true/false, default false; if enabled the app is started and is also started again on system restart, if disabled the app is stopped). show third-party-app-info-<location-id>/<app-name> gives version, state and information per location. third-party-fw is the firmware side: show third-party-fw-<fw-name> with file-status (valid, invalid, missing), path, version, crc, vendor, part-number, nsa-upgrade-version (versions from which upgrade is non-service-affecting), present-in-eqpt and applicable-eqpt (max 80 elements each). To clear it, use clear [-f] app [app-name=]<value>, which clears third party apps. If you want to act on it rather than clear it, appctl [app-name=] [command=] [[target=]] [[parameters=]] controls the app, with command restart, netls or exec, and target defaulting to system.

cli-session-config is the per-session object, and it is what you want: set cli-session-config-<session-id> cli-lines <value>, where cli-lines is the number of rows displayed before the output pauses (range 10..1000, default 40; press SPACEBAR to resume). It also carries cli-columns (80..4000, default 80), interactive-mode (true/false, default true, set per CLI session and not persistent) and display-timestamp (true/false, default false). cli is the management protocol as a whole: set/show cli with enabled (true/false, default true; the CLI cannot be disabled from within a CLI session), port (1..65535, default 22, the ssh listener), script-dir (show only), default-interactive-mode (default true, affecting only newly created sessions) and show-alarm-columns (default default-columns, with a stated global effect on all CLI sessions). The two system-configuration objects are config and extended-config: show config [(<entity-id>|<entity-type>)] displays the system's non-default configuration recursively from the current CLI scope, and add/delete/show extended-config-<name> configures a non-standard extended config, which introduces exceptional behavior globally and requires a name already known to the system.

set is the generic attribute assignment: set [-f|-v] [<entity id>] <attribute> <value> [<attribute> <value> ...] [<filter> ...], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. It needs at least one attribute-value pair, all pairs must belong to the same managed entity, and if no entity id is given the currently scoped entity is used. Wildcards (card-*, port-1-4-*), ranges (card-1-[1..4]) and lists (interface-[DCN,CRAFT]) are supported, -v validates and -f forces; it prompts for confirmation when the request may have traffic impact or implicitly affects multiple instances. The separate operations are: set-alarm-state [state=]<value> [[acknowledge-text=]<value>] (all-alarms | [alarm-id-list=]<value>...), Operational mode, which changes the operator state of an alarm to none, ack or close (state is mandatory), takes 1 up to 10 alarm ids or all-alarms, and stores an optional acknowledge-text of 0..256 characters; and set-time [new-time=]<value>, Operational mode, which changes the system time and is only applicable when time-source is manual, i.e. NTP is not enabled, with an ISO 8601 value such as 2017-01-12T10:22:25Z or +/-hh:mm instead of Z. The one that ends in -set is named-value-set: add/set/show/delete named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value <string 1..1024>].

mc is the Media Channel, a spectrum slot on an OMS: add mc-<name> parent-oms <value> lower-frequency <value> upper-frequency <value>, with center-frequency and slot-width derived by the system (all in MHz), plus label, admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control and auto-delete (default disabled; when enabled the system deletes the MC once no NMC is associated, allowed on RD66TM sleds with l0-mode-op=hsc-ols and always disabled for standard or slte). nmc is the Network Media Channel, the actual carrier-bearing channel: add nmc-<name> parent-facility <value> center-frequency <value>, where parent-facility can be either a Media Channel or an OMS, center-frequency is 190650000..196700000 MHz, width is 15000..200000 MHz (default 35000, and must be set to the 3 dB signal bandwidth matching the transponder baud rate), plus attenuation targets, input-power limits and the ASE insertion attributes. For both, the referenced supporting-card must be part of a Degree, not an ADG. The fillers occupy spectrum that carries no service: mc-f (Media Channel Filler) is show-only, reporting lower-frequency, upper-frequency and slot-width; nmc-f (Network Media Channel Filler) is set/show, with admin-state and alarm-report-control settable and alloc/actual lower and upper frequency and bandwidth (alloc-bandwidth default 75000 MHz), power-actual-tx/rx and monitoring-state readable.

The scan is run by the activate command in Operational mode: activate otdr [entity=]<port> [[otdr-file-prefix=]<value>] triggers a measurement on the target OTDR port, and activate otdr-fiber-check [entity=]<ots-r-id> [[otdr-file-prefix=]<value>] runs a manual OTDR-based fiber check, which executes up to 3 OTDR tests and returns an error if a manual scan or an automatic Raman fiber check is already in progress. You tune how it scans in otdr-ptp: set otdr-ptp-<name> with otdr-range (auto or 0..300.0 km; set it to fiber length plus 10%), otdr-pulse-width (auto or 10..20000 ns), otdr-measurement-speed (fast ~10 s, medium ~15 s, slow ~1 min, precision ~3-5 min, high-precision ~5-7 min, or auto, the default), otdr-ior (auto or 1.0..2.0), otdr-fiber-type (auto by default; SMF-ULL must be configured for the integrated OTDR in RD66TM and D2ILASGM and for HSC-OLS), otdr-resolution (auto or 0.4..100.0), otdr-direction-mode (default counter-prop-in-service), peak-power (auto or 5..14.5) and launching-fiber-length (0..50 m, default 0, deducted from the result). The answer comes out of otdr-ptp too: otdr-fiber-break-distance gives the distance of the break in km, or not-available if none was identified, alongside otdr-last-measurement and otdr-last-measurement-file (the .sor file). Live progress is on the otdr object: otdr-state (not-available, idle, measuring, finished, fail), otdr-measurement-time, otdr-measurement-port, otdr-measurement-direction, otdr-ongoing-measurement-profile and otdr-error. For automatic checks, ots-r-auto-otdr holds automatic-otdr, auto-otdr-state, external-attenuation-rx-measured and total-reflectance-rx-measured.

For the name server, the deciding attribute is origin on dns-server: add/set/show dns-server-<address> [origin <dhcp|manual>], default manual. origin dhcp means the address was assigned to this system by a DHCP server, and origin manual means it was configured by hand; you convert a DHCP-learned entry into a manual one by changing this attribute. What is accepted at all is governed by dns: set dns [assignment-method <manual|dhcp|both>] [enabled <true|false>] [search <string 0..64>], where assignment-method defaults to both, enabled defaults to true, and search must contain at least one dot and is cleared by setting an empty string. A deleted entry that keeps returning is a DHCP-origin entry being re-supplied while assignment-method still admits dhcp. For the relay there are two levels: dhcp-relay is global, set dhcp-relay [mode <disabled|ipv4|ipv6>] [server-address <value>], with mode defaulting to disabled and at least one IPv4 or IPv6 server address required when it is enabled; and if-dhcp-relay is per interface, set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> dhcp-relay-enabled <true|false>, default false, and the guide states it obeys the global dhcp-relay settings. A relay that does nothing is either global mode disabled, no server-address, or dhcp-relay-enabled left false on the interface.

The wipe options live under clear [-f] system [type=]<value> [[target=]<value>] [[restart-behavior=]<value>] [[action=]<value>], Operational mode. type takes three values. factory-reset resets the system or a particular equipment to factory configuration; it stops target traffic services and removes the respective files and user configurations, and may imply loss of connectivity. It does not take effect for 1830 GX G30 Optical Carrier-Cards (OCC2T, OCC2E) but is supported for the G30 controller card (FRCU), and factory-reset with the shutdown option is not supported on L0 cards. full-wipe cleans the entire system and reinstalls the software on the controller and the line cards, stopping all traffic services and removing all files, configurations and software; it implies loss of connectivity and needs a base software reinstall from ONIE to recover. It is not supported for G30 line cards (CHM1R, UTM2) or Optical Carrier-Cards (OCC2T, OCC2E), and is supported for the FRCU only. inactive just clears the inactive software partition. target may be the whole system or a chassis/card AID, defaulting to the entire system, and restart-behavior is restart (default) or shutdown, where shutdown means the system does not restart afterwards. The one that leaves logs and performance data behind is not a clear system option at all: clear [-f] database [[clear-type=]<full|keep-networking|initialize-from-script>] sets the NE database to default and reboots, and the guide states explicitly that it does not wipe logs, PM data and other non-configuration data.

Read show unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name>, which lists inventory detected but not yet accepted by the Node Controller in a multi-chassis configuration. Per entry it gives hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number (string 1..16), clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date and detection-timestamp, the last being the time the Node Controller last detected the unprovisioned equipment. If the slot-name is empty the entry is the chassis itself. Alongside it, show nct-connection-<src-port>/<dst-port> shows the NCT links the system has filled in dynamically, with src-chassis, dst-chassis and src-chassis-state/dst-chassis-state taking node controller, provisioned or unprovisioned, and ports on an unprovisioned chassis appearing in the form <chassis-serial-number>-<slot>-NCT-<id>. On the chassis object itself, show chassis-<name> gives is-node-controller (true/false), chassis-role (unknown, main-chassis, sub-chassis, default unknown) and equipment-discovery-ready, which stays false until all equipment has been discovered during startup. To accept the shelf you add it with add chassis-<name> required-type <G31|G32|G34c|G42> expected-serial-number <value>, expected-serial-number being how you tell the node controller the serial number of a sub-chassis.

control-mode on the amplifier object decides it: set amplifier-<name> control-mode <auto-max-pw|manual>, default auto-max-pw, where auto-max-pw is the automatic mode targeting maximum output power and manual means you set the gain yourself. Whether auto is even offered is reported by amp-control-support (auto, meaning both manual and auto-max-pw are supported, or manual-only). In manual mode you set gain-target (0..40 dB, default 0.0) and gain-range-target (standard, low, high; default standard); gain-range-control follows control-mode automatically, going manual when control-mode is manual and auto when it is auto-max-pw. In auto mode you bias the result with gain-adjustment (-20.00..20.00 dB, default 0, only on amplifiers with function pa or inline). gain-operating reports the gain actually configured, and control-state reports the loop status (unknown, not-applicable, stopped, converged, fine-tuning, adjusting). What would stop it emitting anything: amplifier-enable is disabled by default and must be set to enabled; forced-shutdown set to true forces one amplifier of a dual-band card down; admin-state lock; and even when enabled, output power depends on the existence of the OSC signal for node-type ILA and on the OMS related facilities and the existence of an OXcon for node-type OADM. An input OLOS also triggers a shutdown after olos-shutdown-soak-timer (0..2000 ms, default 0) unless olos-shutdown-disable is true.

Which member is live is read from the protection unit: show protection-unit-<protection-group-name>/<protection-unit-name> [state] [role] [transport-entity]. role is working or protection, and state is active, standby, available or unknown, so the member whose state is active is the one carrying traffic. At the group level, show protection-group-<name> pg-state reports the switching state (no-request, do-not-revert, protection-lockout, frozen, forced-to-working, forced-to-protection, manual-to-working, manual-to-protection, sf-on-working, sf-on-protection, sd-on-working, sd-on-protection, wait-to-restore, unavailable, plus the -remote and exercise variants for bidirectional SNCP; default unavailable), alongside last-switch-trigger, remaining-wtr and switch-failure-reason. The behaviour on a switch is set on protection-group: protection-type (y-cable or snc-n, default y-cable), switching-mode (unidirectional, the default, or bidirectional), reversion-mode (revertive or non-revertive, default non-revertive), hold-off-timer (0..10000 ms in 1 ms steps, default 0), wtr-timer (60..720 s in 1 s steps, default 300, applicable only in revertive mode), pg-request (clear, manual-to-working, manual-to-protection, forced-to-working, forced-to-protection, protection-lockout, exercise; default clear), pg-control-request (freeze or clear-freeze, default clear-freeze), and the four switch triggers client-side-olos-trigger, client-side-sd-trigger, network-side-csf-trigger and network-side-sd-trigger, all enabled/disabled and defaulting to disabled. To force a switch use protection-switch [-f] operation-type=<force|lockout|manual|release> switch-target=<value> protection-group=<value>, where switch-target is not needed for release or lockout.

Trigger the check with verify [-f] type-select=fiber-connection [target-select=<port-id>] [allow-switching], Operational mode. target-select is the port instance-identifier of the CableID-capable card; if it is omitted, all paths are verified. allow-switching is boolean and defaults to false: false verifies active paths only, true also verifies inactive paths by letting the system initiate switching on the OPSM. The pre-condition is that the equipment-policies attribute cable-id-control is set to enabled. The command prompts for confirmation unless -f is used, is non-blocking, and on acceptance raises the CID-verification-in-progress alarm against the NE until all queued test requests complete. Watch progress with show cable-id-status: cable-id-state is idle, running-incl-switching or running-no-switching, and test-progress is a string of the form 'N out of M completed', where M is the total number of port-pairs to be tested and N the number completed. Read the outcome with show cable-id-path-<name>, which gives card-type-a/port-a and card-type-z/port-z (CableID is sourced and terminated only by CAD10A and RD20TM and passes transparently through the OPSM), port-a-to-port-z-path-status and its reverse (enabled/disabled), the two last-test-status attributes (not-verified, pass, fail), current-state, last-test-qualifier (up-to-date or out-dated), last-test-timestamp and additional-info, which names the failure: Cable-ID TxLOS, Cable-ID RxLOS, Cable-ID-MISMATCH for a misconnected fibre, Cable-ID-RxLOF, Power out-of-range, or timeout. show -r cable-id-path-<name> adds the supporting fiber connections. show cable-id lists the CableID entities, and terminate cable-id stops all running verification tests.

Where authentication is sent is decided by security-policies aaa-authentication-method, which defaults to local-only. The remote options are local-first-then-remote (authenticate locally first, then use the remote AAA server), remote-first-then-local (use the remote server first, falling back to local if remote authentication failed or all servers could not be contacted) and remote-unavailable-then-local (use the remote server first, falling back to local only if all servers could not be contacted). If it is still local-only, no request is ever sent to the RADIUS box. The companion attribute aaa-authorization-method (local-only, local-first-then-remote, remote-if-authenticated-else-local, remote-unavailable-then-local; default local-only) governs authorization, and the user must log out and log in again for a change to apply. The server itself is add/set/show/delete aaa-server-<server-name> with protocol-supported (RADIUS, the default, or TACACSPLUS), server-address, server-priority (1..10; if not given, the lowest existing precedence plus 1), server-port (default 49), server-port-authentication (default 1812), server-port-accounting (default 1813), shared-secret (maximum 64 characters, longer values are denied with an error), source-ip, role-supported (authentication, authorization, accounting) and enabled (default true). What happens when it does not answer is governed by timeout, the response timeout for Access-Request messages, range 1..90 seconds, default 5, and retry, the number of attempted Access-Request messages to a single server before failing authentication, range 0..5; the guide notes the total wait time, timeout x (retry + 1), should be less than 5 minutes.

ssh-authorized-key holds the automation account key: add ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> public-key <value> [label <value>]. Each entry is a trusted public key for SSHv2 user authentication; user-name is the owning local or remote user (string 0..32), key-id is a unique name for the entry (string 1..64), and public-key is the OpenSSH public key in PEM form (string 0..2048). public-key-algorithm is show-only and reports ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072 or ssh-rsa4096. For key-based login you must also set security-policies ssh-authentication-method to public-key or public-key-or-password, since the default is password. ssh-known-host holds the remote host the node trusts: add ssh-known-host-<id> address <value> public-key-algorithm <value> public-key <value> [label <value>], where address is the hostname or IPv4/IPv6 address of the allowed peer and public-key-algorithm may additionally be ssh-ed25519 (available from R9.0). How strictly that is enforced is security-policies ssh-strict-host-key-checking, strict or relaxed, default relaxed. The node's own identity is ssh-host-key: show ssh-host-key-<public-key-algorithm> [public-key] [label] [fingerprint-algorithm] [fingerprint], one host key per supported algorithm, auto-generated in the default DB, with fingerprint-algorithm md5 or sha256. Regenerate it with ssh-keygen [-b=<key-length>] [-l=<key-label>] [-t=<rsa|ecdsa|ed25519>], default type rsa; it replaces the existing keys, and with secure-mode enabled RSA supports only 4096 bits and ECDSA 384 or 521 (default 384).

The key agreement policy lives in mka-policy, the MACsec Key Agreement policy referenced by the macsec entity on the Ethernet facility: add/set/show/delete mka-policy-<name> [key-server-priority <value>] [macsec-cipher-suite <value>] [confidentiality-offset <value>] [sak-rekey-interval <value>]. key-server-priority is what the MKA protocol uses to select the key server, macsec-cipher-suite is the cipher suite for Secure Association Key (SAK) derivation, and confidentiality-offset is the number of octets in an Ethernet frame sent as unencrypted plain-text. How often the session key rolls over is sak-rekey-interval, the SAK rekey interval in seconds, range 0 or 30..65535, default 30 s. The per-port MKA instance is macsec-mka: set/show macsec-mka-<name> with mka-policy naming the policy to use, connectivity-association-key and connectivity-association-key-name (the pre-shared CAK and CKN, each string 0..64), psk-lifetime and psk-expiration-warning (range 1..173, default 14 days), psk-lifetime-enable, psk-configured-timestamp, and the read-only is-key-server. You watch the channels themselves with show sc-tx-<name>/<index> and show sc-rx-<name>/<index>, which report sci-tx or sci-rx (a 16-character hex Secure Channel Identifier), state (in-use or not-in-use, as returned by the MKA stack), association-number, key-identifier and next-packet-number. The port-level object macsec-entity carries enabled, link-security-control (must-secure or should-secure, default must-secure), replay-protection, replay-protection-window (0..4294967295, default 0) and the read-only negotiated-cipher-suite.

None of them is off out of the box; enabled defaults to true on all three. netconf: set/show netconf [enabled] [port] [annotate-cli-name] [static-info-in-notifs] [hello-timeout]. port is the ssh listener for NETCONF, uint16 range 1..65535, default 830. hello-timeout is 1..3600 seconds, default 2, and the session is dropped if no hello PDU is received or transmitted in that time. annotate-cli-name defaults to false and annotates the XML output with CLI names. NETCONF cannot be disabled from within a NETCONF session. grpc: set/show grpc [enabled] [port] [gnmi-get-encoding-granularity]. The gNMI over gRPC listener port defaults to 50051, and gnmi-get-encoding-granularity is per-path or per-object, default per-object. The object is system managed and cannot be manually deleted. restconf: set/show restconf [enabled] [http-enabled] [https-enabled] [http-port] [https-port] [cookie-timeout] [api-root]. enabled and https-enabled default to true, while http-enabled defaults to false and HTTP access is not supported in secure mode. http-port defaults to 8080 and https-port to 8181 (both 1..65535), and cookie-timeout is 1..300 minutes, default 5, reset on session activity. For reference the CLI itself listens on port 22 by default.

restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>] is Operational mode and prompts for confirmation unless -f is given. If you omit resource-id it restarts the active controller card, and if you omit type it performs a warm restart, so plain restart card-1-4 is a warm reboot. The three types are: cold, which reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting, with connectivity regained within five minutes; warm, which reboots the processor of the CHM6, UCM4 and similar cards and is non service affecting, also regaining connectivity within five minutes; and shutdown, which gracefully shuts the card down. No, you cannot assume every card behaves the same way. The guide states explicitly that not all cards support all restart types, and it calls out differences: a cold reboot of XMM4 is not service affecting but visibility is lost, whereas a cold reboot of CHM6, UCM4 and similar is service affecting; a warm reboot of XMM4 is non-service affecting but loses visibility for 3 minutes. The restartable entities are card (cold, warm, shutdown), card sub-component (cold, warm) and tom (cold only). List the sub-components with show card resources, then restart one with, for example, restart card-1-4 DCO cold.

Three things must be in place. First, the global switch: set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates <enabled|disabled>, which defaults to disabled. Application of serdes-templates depends on this flag being true; on enabling, templates are not applied retroactively, only from that moment onward, and on disabling there is no impact because the existing serdes configuration is kept on all TOMs regardless of how it was applied. Second, the template itself: add serdes-template-<name> [tom-part-number <string 1..16>] [card-types-applicable <value>] [ports-applicable <value>]. Templates are created per tom-part-number and apply to all line cards that support serdes; ports-applicable is a list of up to 20 port names or all, which is the default. When a TOM with that part-number is plugged in, the template is applied automatically. Third, the actual parameter values: add serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name> value <value>, one entry per serdes parameter name and value, for example RxAmplitude, RxEQ, TxEQ, RxPreCursor, RxPostCursor, TxEQAdaptive. The card must also support it: show supported-card-<card-type> support-serdes-config must be true, which means the card-type allows 3rd party TOM SerDes values to be configured (default false). Manual serdes configuration via add/set serdes-<card-name>-<port-name>/<serdes-name> value <value> is still allowed and is kept even where it deviates from the template. Swapping in a TOM with a different part-number resets the serdes configuration and re-applies the new template if one exists, and apply-template forces re-application.

ots is the Optical Transport Section, the fibre span itself: set/show ots-<name> carries fiber-type-rx/fiber-type-tx, fiber-length-rx/fiber-length-tx (with fiber-length-derived-rx/tx), raman-coefficient-rx/tx, span-loss-reference, span-loss-transmit/span-loss-receive, span-loss-derived and span-loss-baseline, span-loss-alarm-threshold, span-loss-aging-margin-rx, external-attenuation-tx/rx, target-power-setting, target-power-adjust-cband and -lband, osc-compatibility, osc-less and osc-less-support, enable-dcn-interworking, laser-safety-mode and loading-policy. oms is the Optical Multiplex Section, the multiplexed band riding on the OTS: monitoring-mode (not-monitored, intrusive, non-intrusive, dge-fixed-attenuation, ila-with-equalization, integrated-equalization; default intrusive for all node types except ILA, not-monitored for ILA, integrated-equalization for hyperscale ILA), grid-mode (flexible by default, or fixed-50G-96ch, fixed-100G-48ch, fixed-75G-64ch, fixed-75G-64ch-oif, fixed-50G-7100, fixed-150G-40ch), lower-frequency 191300000 MHz and upper-frequency 196150000 MHz by default, band-allowed/band-actual/band-target, assigned-degree, wss-less and target-output-power (5.00..20.00 dBm, default 5). ops is the Optical Physical Section at the port: role is tributary, multi-carrier, general-purpose (default), ase-input or active-multi-carrier, with supported-roles reported by the system, input-psd-profile (-30..-6 dBm/12.5GHz, default -6) and port-expansion (no or y-cable, for Y-cable expansion). osc is the Optical Supervisory Channel and it is the one carrying the supervisory traffic: osc-mode is OC3 (155 Mbit/s) or 1GE with FEC (1.25 Gbit/s, HSC OLS nodes only), l0-comm-interface-type selects ipv4 or ipv6 for inter-NE communication, and it has osc-control (auto or manual, default auto), target-output-power (-2.5..4.5 dBm), tx-power-adjustment (-6..6 dB), voa-attenuation-target-rx (0..30 dB, default 10), osc-wavelength and lof-soak-timer (short, about 3 ms, or long, adding about 2300 ms).

The behaviour is configured on the tributary client physical termination point: set trib-ptp-<name> tributary-disable-action <value>. That attribute states what the network element does towards the client equipment connected over the TOM when a line-side failure is observed, either shutting off the laser or inserting a replacement signal. The default is laser-shut-off, and the other values are none, odu-ais, send-ais-1, send-gais, send-idles, send-lf, send-ms-ais and send-nos (the last for 1830 GX G30 only). So by default the node turns the client laser off. You delay that with tributary-disable-holdoff-timer, the hold-off time for client shutdown or replacement signal in the egress direction, uint16 range 0..10000 milliseconds, default 0 meaning the hold-off functionality is disabled; the guide notes it applies only when the TDA action is laser-turnoff, holding the optical signal as it is until the timer expires before turning the laser off. Related switches on the same object are near-end-tda (enabled/disabled, default disabled), tda-degrade-mode (enabled/disabled, default disabled, for BERSD-ODU triggering ALS) and forward-defect-trigger (true/false, default true), which decides whether a received client forward defect such as LF or ODU-AIS flows through to the line side or instead triggers an egress TDA action. Example: set trib-ptp-1-5-T2 tributary-disable-action laser-shut-off.
